title: Viktor: AI Coworker That Lives in Slack — Fryderyk Wiatrowski
talk_summary: Fryderyk Wiatrowski describes Viktor, a Slack-native company AI employee that inherits shared integrations and context from one connector, and outlines the hard problems: multi-user memory, channel-scoped context isolation, mapping many Slack interaction modes into a linear context, and model personality. The talk is mostly product narrative, but a few mechanisms (scoped/shared integrations, context rollover across threads, personality as a model-selection criterion, staged proactivity rollout) are copyable.

takeaways.what_they_do: When a user abandons a Slack thread and starts a fresh DM, the agent looks back at prior messages and rolls that context into the existing conversation instead of treating it as a brand-new task/sandbox.
Integrations are shared company-wide by default (one connector serves everyone), but they added per-user scoping so personal credentials are only usable in that person's DMs, not company-wide.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we added a capability to Victor to kind of scope the integrations. So, they're not always shared

takeaways.what_they_do: They A/B tested GPT-5.4 vs Opus for Viktor; GPT was cheaper and good at tool-calling/codegen, but users revolted over personality, so they kept Opus as the main model.
takeaways.evidence_quote: on the tool calling and code gen, it's actually amazing... and it's actually cheaper as well... one the most interesting one is the personality

takeaways.what_they_do: Proactive behavior (agent jumping into threads unprompted) caused security alarm on day one, so they gate proactivity: earn it with a few users first, then roll out slowly.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if Victor does it on day one... the security team start raging... earn it with the first use with a few users first and then you can roll it out slowly

takeaways.what_they_do: They treat memory as the top challenge when one agent serves many users/channels, and enforce that context from one channel (e.g. growth/exec) does not leak into another (engineering/support) or into DMs of non-members.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you somehow need to make sure that this context will not be leaked to the engineering or support channel

takeaways.what_they_do: They chose Slack over a web app partly because 10-minute agent tasks feel unacceptable in a chat UI but acceptable as a Slack request to a 'coworker', changing perceived latency.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you ping someone on Slack and tell them to build an app for you and get an answer in 10 minutes, you are shocked
